prompt: Which of boxoffice's values does the lesson keep in code rather than make configurable?

choices.text: The connection pool size, since it depends on the database
choices.why: The pool varies with the database's limit and the number of copies, so it is configuration.

choices.text: `ReadHeaderTimeout`
choices.why: Right. No environment wants a Slowloris defence of thirty seconds, so a setting only adds a way to get it wrong.

choices.text: The HTTP address
choices.why: A container must listen on every interface, so the address differs between environments.

choices.text: The site allowed to call the API
choices.why: A staging site is a different site, so it varies.

prompt: What test does the lesson give for whether a value is configuration?

choices.text: It is a number, such as a port or a timeout
choices.why: Numbers such as the header timeout stay in code; being a number decides nothing.

choices.text: Somebody once asked for it to be changeable without a release
choices.why: A request is not a difference between environments.

choices.text: It differs between environments; the code does not
choices.why: Right. Configuration is what legitimately differs.

choices.text: It appears in more than one file
choices.why: Appearing twice is a reason to read it once, not a test of whether it varies.

prompt: Why does the lesson refuse a setting such as `BOXOFFICE_ENV=production` that code branches on?

choices.text: Environment names are longer than the variable limit
choices.why: No such limit is involved; the problem is the code path.

choices.text: Go cannot compare strings read from the environment
choices.why: It compares them like any other string.

choices.text: The flag package rejects variables that name an environment
choices.why: The flag package knows nothing about environment names.

choices.text: A production-only branch is first exercised by real users
choices.why: Right. Environments differ in values, never in which lines run.

prompt: Order boxoffice's sources of a setting from the one that is overridden by everything to the one that overrides everything.
items: a flag on the command line

prompt: `./knobs -max-conns ten` stops with the help. What exit status does it end with?

choices.text: 0, the same as `-h`
choices.why: `-h` exits with 0 because asking for help is not an error; a bad value is.
The transcript printed `exit 2`.

choices.text: 127, as for a command that does not exist
choices.why: 127 is the shell's status for a missing command, not the flag package's.
Right. The flag package uses 2 for a command line used wrong.

prompt: `./knobs report.csv -v` printed `verbose: false`. Why?

choices.text: `-v` must come with `=true`
choices.why: A bool flag on its own means true, as the second run showed.

choices.text: Parsing stopped at `report.csv`
choices.why: Right. Both `report.csv` and `-v` landed in `flag.Args()`.

choices.text: Flags written after a file name apply to that file and not to the program
choices.why: The package has no notion of flags belonging to a file.

choices.text: `-v` is reserved for the version
choices.why: `knobs` declared `-v` itself, and the package reserves only `-h` and `-help`.

prompt: `./knobs -v false -addr :9000` left the address at its default. What happened?
hint: A bool takes a value only one way.

choices.text: The package reported an error and used the defaults
choices.why: Nothing complained; that is the trap.

choices.text: `false` ended the parsing before `-addr`
choices.why: Right. Only `-v=false` gives a bool flag a value.

choices.text: `false` was read as the value of `-v` and `:9000` was refused
choices.why: The output shows `verbose: true` and `:9000` among the leftover arguments.

choices.text: Two flags in one command conflict
choices.why: The second run set three flags at once without trouble.

prompt: Match each command line to what `knobs` made of it.
How does the `flag` package read `-xvf`?
hint: It is not a GNU tool.

choices.text: As one flag named `xvf`
choices.why: Right. Programs that want combined short flags use `pflag` or `cobra`.

choices.text: As the flags `-x`, `-v` and `-f`
choices.why: That is the GNU style, which `spf13/pflag` adds.

choices.text: As `-x` with the value `vf`
choices.why: The package never splits a flag's name.

choices.text: As a subcommand named `xvf`
choices.why: Subcommands come from `cobra`, and they have no dash.

prompt: Why does boxoffice use `flag.NewFlagSet` instead of `flag.String` and `flag.Parse`?

choices.text: The global set parses faster
choices.why: Speed is not the difference; where the arguments come from is.

choices.text: The global set rejects duration flags
choices.why: `knobs` declared `-wait` as a duration on the global set.

choices.text: Its own set parses a slice it is given
choices.why: Right. The global set reads `os.Args`, and any package declares flags on it at will.

choices.text: Only a set made with `NewFlagSet` prints the help text for `-h`
choices.why: `knobs` used the global set and printed help.

prompt: `BOXOFFICE_REGION= ./knobs` printed `"", set: true`. What would `os.Getenv` have returned?
hint: It has one result, not two.

choices.text: An error saying the variable is empty
choices.why: `os.Getenv` returns no error.

choices.text: `""`, as if unset
choices.why: Right. Only `LookupEnv` tells the two apart.

choices.text: `nil`
choices.why: It returns a string, and a string is never nil.

choices.text: The value the shell had before this command overrode it
choices.why: The command set it to nothing for this run.

prompt: Why does boxoffice treat an empty variable as unset?
hint: A container definition with nothing after `=`.

choices.text: Go cannot store an empty variable in a process's environment
choices.why: `LookupEnv` reported one in the transcript.

choices.text: Empty variables are not passed to child processes
choices.why: They are passed like any other.

choices.text: Empty almost always means left blank
choices.why: Right. Nobody means the site to be the empty string.

choices.text: `fs.Set` refuses an empty string for every type
choices.why: A string flag accepts one; the choice is boxoffice's.

prompt: Why does `DATABASE_URL` keep its name without the `BOXOFFICE_` prefix?

choices.text: A prefix would make it a flag
choices.why: Names of variables have nothing to do with flags.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses connections from prefixed names
choices.why: PostgreSQL never sees the variable's name.

choices.text: Other tools read it by that name
choices.why: Right. Well-known names stay as they are; the program's own settings get the prefix.

choices.text: It is a secret, and secrets never carry a prefix
choices.why: `BOXOFFICE_MANAGER_TOKEN` is a secret with the prefix.

prompt: boxoffice is running, and you change `BOXOFFICE_ORIGIN` in its shell. What happens?

choices.text: The next request uses the new site
choices.why: The running process keeps the environment it started with.

choices.text: boxoffice exits, because its environment changed
choices.why: A process is never told about a change in its parent's shell.

choices.text: Open WebSockets switch to the new site and others keep the old one
choices.why: No part of the process reads the variable again.

choices.text: Nothing, until it restarts
choices.why: Right. A variable is read once, at start-up.

prompt: The user `nobody` ran `ps` against `knobs`. What could it see?

choices.text: Nothing, because the process belongs to ana
choices.why: It printed the whole command line.

choices.text: The arguments, `hunter2` included
choices.why: Right. Every user reads every command line; `/proc/PID/environ` is for the owner and root.

choices.text: The environment and the command line
choices.why: Reading `environ` as `nobody` gave `Permission denied`.

choices.text: Only the program's name, with the arguments masked
choices.why: The arguments came out whole.

prompt: boxoffice reads a secret from a variable, or from the path held in a twin variable whose name ends in ___.
The tokens sit in `~/.profile`, and only ana and root can read `/proc/PID/environ`. What is still wrong with that arrangement?

choices.text: Every program ana starts receives them, and anything that prints its environment prints them
choices.why: Right. A file only its owner reads reaches only the process that opens it.

choices.text: Variables are lost when the terminal closes
choices.why: `~/.profile` sets them again in every new terminal; that is the problem, not loss.

choices.text: `ps` shows exported variables to every user
choices.why: `ps` showed the arguments; the environment was refused to `nobody`.

choices.text: Go reads only the first ten variables
choices.why: Go reads all of them.

prompt: Why does section 08 write the token file inside `(umask 077; …)`?

choices.text: `openssl` refuses to write without it
choices.why: `openssl rand` writes under any umask.

choices.text: So the file is born private
choices.why: Right. A `chmod` afterwards leaves a moment when the file was readable.

choices.text: It encrypts the file
choices.why: A umask only sets permissions; the file is plain text, `-rw-------`.

choices.text: To change ana's umask for every later terminal
choices.why: The parentheses make a subshell, so the umask ends with it.

prompt: How many modules did `go get github.com/spf13/viper@v1.21.0` add to an empty project?
An empty program that only imports Viper came out at 6.3 MB. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: For seven settings, `flag` and `os.Getenv` do the job
choices.why: Right. Sixty readable lines against 13 modules you ship.

choices.text: Viper is broken and has to be avoided in every program
choices.why: The lesson calls it a fair price for a tool with dozens of settings in several formats.

choices.text: Size is irrelevant once the binary is stripped
choices.why: The cost includes the modules you update and trust, not only bytes.

choices.text: A configuration file is always better than variables
choices.why: A file earns its place only when settings stop being flat.

prompt: How does the lesson have a `.env` file reach boxoffice?

choices.text: boxoffice reads `.env` beside its binary at start-up
choices.why: That would be a second way in that works only on developers' machines.

choices.text: The shell loads it with `set -a; . ./.env; set +a`
choices.why: Right. The program reads the environment as always.

choices.text: It is committed, and `go build` embeds it
choices.why: A `.env` is never committed; `.env.example` goes in its place.

choices.text: Through a `-env` flag
choices.why: boxoffice declares no such flag.

prompt: In `load`, how does a flag on the command line end up beating its `BOXOFFICE_*` variable?

choices.text: `Parse` runs first and `VisitAll` skips flags already set
choices.why: `VisitAll` runs first; `Parse` comes last.

choices.text: `Parse` runs after `VisitAll` has applied the variables
choices.why: Right. Each step overwrites the one before.

choices.text: The flag package always prefers a flag to a variable of the same name
choices.why: The package knows nothing of variables; the order of the code decides.

choices.text: `errors.Join` keeps the last value
choices.why: `errors.Join` joins errors, not values.

prompt: Why does `load` take `getenv func(string) string` instead of calling `os.Getenv`?

choices.text: `os.Getenv` is unsafe in `main`
choices.why: `main` passes exactly `os.Getenv`.

choices.text: A function reads variables faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: The flag package demands it
choices.why: The flag package never reads the environment.

choices.text: So a test passes a map instead
choices.why: Right. `main` passes `os.Getenv`; a test passes its own function.

prompt: Why does `load` collect problems in a slice and return `errors.Join`?

choices.text: Go forbids returning an error from inside a loop
choices.why: Go has no such rule.

choices.text: `errors.Join` hides the secrets
choices.why: Hiding is `secret`'s job.

choices.text: Whoever fixes it sees every problem at once, not one per restart
choices.why: Right. The refusal in section 08 listed five lines.

choices.text: So the program starts with the valid settings and skips the rest
choices.why: Any error means boxoffice does not start.

prompt: Match each check in `load` to the reason behind it.
hint: They are about what boxoffice needs.

pairs.right: a browser's `Origin` header always has one
without one no staff could sign in

prompt: `secret` has `LogValue` and `String`. What still shows the real value?

choices.text: `slog.Info` with the secret as a value
choices.why: `LogValue` makes that `[hidden]`.

choices.text: `fmt.Printf("%v", cfg)`
choices.why: `String` makes that `[hidden]`.

choices.text: `string(cfg.DatabaseURL)`
choices.why: Right. `main` converts it at the one place the real value is needed.

choices.text: `config`'s own `LogValue`
choices.why: It passes the secret through `slog.Any`, which hides it.

prompt: boxoffice started with `BOXOFFICE_MAX_CONNS=4` and `-max-conns 6`. What `max_conns` did its first log line show?
The refusal in section 08 printed five lines for four deliberate mistakes. Where did the fifth come from?

choices.text: The flag package added its own line
choices.why: No flag was given; all five lines are `load`'s.

choices.text: `errors.Join` repeats the first error
choices.why: All five lines differ.

choices.text: The terminal had no manager token
choices.why: Right. A new terminal without the export has no token.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refused the connection
choices.why: Nothing started, so nothing connected.

prompt: What does boxoffice do when `load` returns `flag.ErrHelp`?

choices.text: It prints the error and exits with 2
choices.why: That is what every other error does.

choices.text: It returns, ending with status 0
choices.why: Right. The help was already printed, and asking for it is not a failure.

choices.text: It starts with the defaults
choices.why: It does not start at all.

choices.text: It logs the configuration and exits
choices.why: The configuration is logged only after `load` succeeds.

prompt: Which statements match this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: boxoffice declares no flag for a secret
choices.why: Right. A command line is readable by every user.

choices.text: `-h` documents each setting's variable too
choices.why: Right. `VisitAll` adds the variable's name to the help.

choices.text: An unreadable file named by `_FILE` falls back to the plain variable
choices.why: It is an error, never a quiet fallback.

choices.text: `BOXOFFICE_WRITE_TIMEOUT` and `-write-timeout` use different parsers
choices.why: `fs.Set` uses the flag's own parser for the variable.

prompt: A colleague wants to pass the database password as `-db-password` so it is visible in the help. What does the lesson answer?

choices.text: No: every user reads it with `ps`; it goes in a file named by `DATABASE_URL_FILE`
choices.why: Right. A file only its owner reads, named by the variable.

choices.text: Fine, as long as the help hides the default
choices.why: The value on a running command line is the problem, not the help.

choices.text: No: flags are limited to 64 characters
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: Fine, if it is also in `.env`
choices.why: Two places for one secret doubles the exposure.

log the configuration it started with
